Dear SaaStr: How Do Startups Really Sell to Big Enterprises Before They’re Proven? You solve their problems. And you solve a specific problem that is important to your buyer — that the existing, current, proven vendors don’t solve well. Large enterprises use lots of tools, widgets, and software in their businesses, but they tend to use the obvious, trusted solutions. At least 90% of the time. They aren’t looking for a cheaper version of ServiceNow or a slicker version of Salesforce, for example. But they are looking for two things, which allows start-ups to break though into big companies before they have brands:
True innovation in their core processes
. Almost all big companies now have innovation departments of some sort, as do many divisions and groups. The general idea is to bring in 1–2 new vendors a year that don’t risk taking the core business down, but could have a material impact on the bottom line. Solving certain top headaches
. Big companies do have budget to solve their headaches. If your solution solves a procurement or sales or finance or HR or whatever headache, and you hit the buyer at the right time, you can get a meeting. And often a sale. Is this hard? Yes. So can an eight-person startup sell to a Fortune 1000 company? Absolutely! In fact, almost every leading B2B vendor started out selling to large customers early.  Zoom did.  Slack did.  Datadog did.  HubSpot did.  Even Shopify sold to its largest customer ever — Walmart — literally within weeks after launch!
But here’s the thing: those deals happened because someone had done the actual work of understanding what mattered to that particular enterprise buyer. Not just built another feature. Built relationships. Built trust. Earned credibility. Demonstrated value so compelling that even without brand recognition, the business case became impossible to ignore. The question isn’t whether your size will stop you. It’s whether anyone inside the organization actually believes you might matter enough to justify the time required to learn more. And the answer depends entirely on how you show up. Because regardless of your logo, your ARR, or your funding rounds—if you can demonstrate genuine expertise around solving their problems—you’ll find doors opening where others assumed walls stood. That’s the beauty of building B2B software. Sometimes, the best product wins. More often, the product that solves the biggest pain point wins. And sometimes—especially these days—it’s the company willing to earn its place in the conversation. That takes grit, persistence, and willingness to listen. But if you’re prepared to put in the work, your company size won’t hold you back. The real constraint is usually only whether someone will give you a chance to prove it.
answer_b:
So after $100m+ invested, I’ve learned one thing for sure about selling to enterprise customers …
It’s tough. It’s much easier to sell to SMBs than to large enterprises … until you get good at it.  Because larger deals mean more people involved in buying decisions, longer cycles, more scrutiny — and even higher expectations. But also because bigger deals lead to bigger wins. To prove out your product in real-world deployments. To show traction. To build confidence. And especially today, with so many AI-fueled disruptions, it’s never too early to go Enterprise. Too many startups think going enterprise is only possible once they’ve crossed $20-$30 million ARR or later. Even earlier, say around $5-$7 million, when growth starts slowing somewhat due to natural barriers. But I see a lot of mistakes here, and a lot of unnecessary friction. In particular, I’m seeing far too many B2B / SaaS startups trying to sell to enterprises without understanding the social contract. What’s the social contract between you and potential buyers? It’s simple: you need to earn trust. Earn it by showing up every day, delivering value consistently, building relationships, solving real problems, and demonstrating that you’re a partner—not just another vendor. I remember a couple years ago in the early days of SaaStr Fund, I was interviewing a portfolio company and they had three different types of revenue streams, okay? Three different products, very interesting, like, 50% in one category, 25% in another, 25% in a third. It was complicated. In fact, it was almost like a startup within a startup. And I asked him, "Tell me how to model it. Tell me how to model each segment." He said, "Well, let me call my VP of Sales and he'll set up a meeting for us."
He didn't understand the social contract. He thought his job was to generate demand. His job wasn't to help me understand the product, understand the business. He didn't understand the social contract. All I wanted to know was what are the chances you're going to hit the plan? Not whether you were growing or shrinking. This changes the rest of our lives. And that's real competition.
answer_b: I've been doing a lot of investing lately and I always cringe when I see teaser decks. It's like sending an unsolicited email. Put all the information in the deck. What I did, I took 50 of my favorite companies, including Salesforce, Twilio, Datadog, Workday, Zendesk, Talkdesk, HubSpot, Qualtrics, Asana, Okta, Pagerduty, Box, RingCentral, etc., and looked at every single one of them and said, "Okay, what were the top three reasons you invested?" Because you never asked me directly, but I think that would help answer the question. And I was surprised how similar the answers were. And I boiled them down to five things. Let me share those because that will give you a framework. First, it had to be a good person running the thing. It didn't have to be perfect, but it has to be a good person. Second, it had to be a clear leader. Third, it had to be a big addressable market. Fourth, it had to be happy customers. Fifth, it had to be repeatable revenue. Those are the same criteria today as they were in 2010. Even though maybe the metrics change. Maybe the markets expand differently. But those remain the core criteria. Um, let me add another layer on it. When you're selling to a buyer who isn't the end user, especially a corporate buyer, a procurement manager, a head of IT, whatever it is, whoever the buyer is, it's not the end customer. They probably won't understand your product. They will buy products they already use. They will buy products that fit within their budget. They will buy products that align with the overall strategy of the corporation.

Master Your Product and Market

A little while back we had a session at our first digital event,
SaaStr Scale
on how to truly stand out during a job interview.
From SDR to VP of Sales, each panelist shared what made them stand out in any given interview.
First off, there were so many good suggestions, but here are my Top 10 learnings from the sessions and Q&A that really stood out to me:

#1.  Know the Product Cold
I was surprised so many senior execs didn’t know the product before an interview.  But all the best ones did.  And it makes a huge difference.
#2.  Don’t Just Talk About the Good Stuff.  Share the Bad Stuff, too.  Especially When You Were Wrong
We’ve talked about this again and again over the years, but it still holds.  So many folks like to hide their mistakes, even as CEOs.  That doesn’t help anyone.  Instead, highlight some things you got wrong … and what you learned from it.  This always helps.
#3.  Show Up Early.  Always.  And Bring Coffee / Water / Etc.
This isn’t rocket science, but so many folks forget to do this.  Even now, Zooming into meetings late.
#4.  Ask for Time to Prepare
If you haven’t done enough research beforehand, ask for extra time to prepare after the formal part of the interview.  Everyone gets these requests, and no one minds.
#5.  Do Real Homework Ahead Of Time
Many of us skip doing real homework ahead of time.  But the very best job applicants do this.  Find out who else has interviewed, what they are working on, what the challenges are today, etc.  And share that in the interview.
#6.

A little bit of both is fine, but again, most of my best investments were made before the product launch. Before the product launched, I had the ability to pick the co-founder and pick the CEO. As soon as you start selling, you have to start making decisions based on data. What's working? What isn't? Who needs to go? Who needs to stay? It becomes less about vision and strategy and more about execution. So, be careful. Being a manager means becoming a decision-maker. Don't confuse the two. Again, I'm not saying you shouldn't have ideas. You absolutely should. But when you start managing teams, you're gonna need to make tough calls quickly. You cannot do this without having worked at a startup for 18 months minimum. Not four years ago. Not last week. Here's the thing. Many times, you'll hear in interviews, "Oh, yeah, I've managed big teams. I've managed hundreds of people." Oh, cool. That sounds awesome. But if you haven't done it at a startup where it's close quarters, where you're talking to customers daily, where failure feels real, then you don't actually understand what it takes to manage people at a startup. Managing people at a big tech company is fundamentally different from managing people at a startup. Different goals, different timelines, different resources. answer_a:
Q: How do I know my SaaS company isn’t an “NRR zombie”?
Here’s how to figure it out:
First, calculate your Net Revenue Retention Rate (NRR). It’s calculated by dividing the total revenue from retained accounts by the original contract value over a one-year period. For example, let’s say you started with $10M ARR and grew to $15M after a year, but through upsells or price increases that came mostly from smaller accounts. In that case, your NRR would be 150%. Now here’s where it gets tough:
If your NRR is above 115%-118%, you’re probably fine. But if it’s consistently lower than that, you might be heading into zombie territory. And if it’s under 110%, you need help – fast. Here’s why:
At 90%+ NRR, you’ve basically become a bank. You’re just collecting interest on existing relationships rather than building new ones. That means every dollar you spend on marketing, sales, and R&D is essentially burning cash because you’re not growing your core business. The only way to recover? Massive layoffs, massive cuts to R&D … or finding a way to reignite product-market fit. Unfortunately, most companies try to fix this problem with cost-cutting instead of fixing their products. They cut their teams down to size while pretending nothing’s wrong. Meanwhile, their competitors keep innovating, hiring great people, and actually delivering value to customers. By the time they realize what happened, they’re too far behind to catch up.
answer_b:
The NRR Zombie is when you see an SaaS company that has great revenue retention (NRR), but isn’t growing any faster than its NRR + 10%-15%. This often happens around $5m-$6m ARR or so, and I’ve seen it again-and-again. The core metrics look good:
Strong net revenue retention — say 105%-115%
Growing reasonably quickly
Happy customers, with low churn
But … But …
Growth slows down after $Xm ARR
The CEO gets tired / burned out
Customer count doesn’t really increase much anymore
New bookings slow way down
This is actually worse than a “Burning Ship” scenario. At least there, everyone knows things are tough. At least, most investors understand that the competition is stronger than expected. And importantly, at least, no one expects things to get better anytime soon. With a BURNING SHIP, you know where you stand. And the VCs will write checks just to keep the ship from sinking. But an NRR zombie? It looks like success. Just not enough success. So what do you do here? A few thoughts:

#1.  NRR is destiny.
When NRR drops below 110%, alarm bells should go off. Below 100%, you’re in serious trouble. Monitor this metric religiously.  And also realize when your team starts lying to you about it.  Even small dips can be a sign something is amiss.

Your CFO is being transparent, which is good, but the repeated misses suggest there may be underlying problems with forecasting, cash management, or burn rate planning. Start by reviewing and refining your monthly forecasts. Identify patterns, trends, and seasonality in your business. Are there specific categories of expenses that tend to balloon unexpectedly? Once you identify the problem spots, work together to implement controls and mitigate them. Fourth, consider bringing in external help
If your CFO lacks experience managing budgets in a high-growth environment, it might be worth exploring additional support. This could be an internal promotion, an outside consultant, or even considering replacing your current CFO.

everything

A VP of Engineering gets on a discovery call. They ask a simple technical question: “How does your API handle rate limiting at scale?”
The SDR freezes. “That’s a great question! Let me connect you with our solutions engineer who can dive deep into the technical details.”
This happens 95% of the time.

The SDR didn’t know the answer. Didn’t even pretend to. Sent someone else over instead. Lost the deal because they couldn’t demonstrate basic product understanding during discovery. This isn’t incompetence—it’s structural. Most B2B companies hire SDRs based on personality and communication skills rather than actual domain expertise. Then they expect these generalists to sell complex technical products to sophisticated buyers. The result is predictable: long delays while someone “gets back to us,” awkward moments where the SDR admits they’re out of their depth, and lost opportunities because competitors (often startups) already knew the answers cold. When we built our first AI SDR at SaaStr, we thought we were giving away free money. Now we realize we were giving away unfair advantages—because everyone else was still doing things the broken way. Our process starts with a working human SDR motion. You need something to clone. Someone who understands your ICP, your messaging framework, and your core objections. But once you have that foundation, the AI takes over everything else. Daily Management Requirements
Every morning, you spend 30 minutes reviewing output. Not quality control—you’re looking for patterns. Which prospects did it write perfect emails to versus generic templates? Where did it struggle? Why?

Then find the right specialist (human or AI) to implement it. Or maybe even hire both, simultaneously. You'll spend less money overall and build something that actually generates ROI rather than burning cash on a solution looking for a problem to solve.

Q: What do most investors look for when evaluating startups for investment?

Most investors evaluate startups based on several key factors:

Growth Rate (ARR)
Market Size and Potential
Competitive Advantage (Moat)
Management Team Experience
Product-Market Fit
Scalability and Efficiency
Financial Projections and Sustainability
Product Vision and Differentiation
Traction and Customer Validation
Investors use frameworks like the "Three Cs" to assess these factors:

Cohort Quality and Repeat Business
Customer Count and Expansion Rates
Conversion Rates and Lifetime Value
These metrics provide insights into product-market fit, customer adoption, and revenue potential.

However, different stages require different evaluation criteria. For early-stage startups, traction and market validation are crucial. Later-stage companies must demonstrate proven business models and execution capabilities.

So I’ve been doing a lot of research lately on AI and how different leaders are using it across the board — from Palantir, HubSpot, Salesforce, Zendesk, ServiceNow, Monday.com and so many other leaders.
One thing keeps jumping out at me:  while everyone talks about how great AI is … and it really is great …
No one is perfect yet.
Not even close.
Everyone still needs humans to help with issues, questions, problems, etc.  Everyone still needs humans to manage complex deployments, migrations, integrations, rollouts, etc.  Everything in tech today is faster and easier with AI, but none of it automates itself.
And importantly, no matter how great things look, especially early, almost every single leader in B2B/SaaS I talk to sees some level of decay over time.  Some is expected — there are always bugs, issues, gaps in workflows, etc.  Others seem like they might be solvable with more investment, but aren’t fixed yet.
I’m not sure if AI apps are just inherently less stable, or if it’s because of the pace of change, or what.  But I think it’s worth being aware of.
It’s also why I think the best way to use AI Agents is to start off using them to do the easy parts first.  Try to automate any repetitive tasks, like updating CRM records, sending emails, etc.  Those are often simple enough to work well with AI agents.  Then add more complexity step-by-step.
I see too many folks trying to jump straight to complex business process automation too quickly, and having trouble.  Just take it a few steps at a time, and push through the bumps and rough spots.
Finally, realize that you’ll need a team of experts to manage your AI Agent deployments.  Not necessarily for each agent, but overall.  We hired a full-time employee to manage our vibe coding platform, and another full-time employee to manage our AI agents.  Both are critical and require constant management.

This revelation might lead you to question whether you’re truly building a technology company or operating a distribution organization masquerading as tech. The Uncomfortable Truth About SaaS Business Models
Let’s examine why this dichotomy exists and what it means for your company’s future. The Two Fundamental Approaches
Traditional Tech Companies (Apple, Google)
Build proprietary platforms and ecosystems
Create switching costs through integration
Focus on product excellence and user experience
Profitability comes from differentiated products and customer loyalty
Distribution Organizations (Amazon, Shopify)
Collect fees for facilitating transactions between buyers and sellers
Value proposition is convenience and accessibility
Survival depends on network effects and scale advantages
Profitability requires massive volume and minimal differentiation
Why Your SaaS Business Might Be More Distribution Than Tech
Your customers don’t buy software; they buy solutions to problems. While your platform provides the underlying infrastructure, the actual value lies in how users interact with the system. Think back to your early days – wasn’t it challenging to onboard new customers because your product was too technical? The problem isn’t the technology itself; it’s the complexity barrier preventing adoption. Once overcome, however, customers become dependent on your solution rather than any particular feature. This creates predictable revenue patterns similar to traditional subscription models, masking the true nature of your business.

And also, because they didn’t really know what they were buying.

answer_b:
Dear SaaStr: Is it Bad to Leave a Struggling Startup?
There’s nothing wrong with leaving a struggling start-up. In fact, there’s actually something kind of empowering about it. If you’re doing well (i.e., making good money), you might feel guilty leaving.  Many times, if you’ve worked somewhere before, you’ll run into old bosses or colleagues at another start-up, especially in the SF Bay Area.  They may assume you left without giving notice, etc.  But if you didn’t leave without cause — you weren’t fired — it was OK. In fact, there’s even a certain zen in knowing it wasn’t you. Sometimes it just isn’t you. Sometimes it’s the job itself. Sometimes it’s even the mission, goals, and values themselves. If the startup has 10+ employees and decent funding, you’re probably better off moving on. You’ll likely end up happier, more productive, and ultimately more successful. Why? Because:
Your energy won’t be wasted
. When you stay at a failing start-up, you’ll inevitably burn out trying to fix problems that are beyond repair. Your efforts will be futile, and your mental health will suffer. Moving on allows you to redirect your energy toward opportunities where you can actually succeed. You’ll avoid toxic dynamics
. Failing start-ups can become toxic environments, where everyone feels like they’re walking on eggshells. Leaving early helps you avoid the emotional toll of watching everything unravel while feeling trapped. You’ll maintain relationships
. Staying at a failing start-up can damage your professional network.

2. On acquiring customers consistently
You may not have that magical sales person, but as a founder, you simply have to sell. Here’s the trick with founder lead sales: customers and prospects love to talk to the CEO. If you can solve a prospect’s problem and you are the CEO leverage that. You don’t have to be the World’s Best Salesperson to sell as a founder, you just have to try to sell. And then, there are your superpowers. In those early days, founders are good at one or two aspects— these are what work well for your company. These are what Jason calls your superpowers. For instance, when Algolia was trying to get off the ground, the co-founder Nicolas Dessaigne often got on the stage at events, which generated a lot of buzz and product interest. He would also attend developer networking events and man a booth. His consistent efforts paid off when Algolia became a known brand among developers. Julien Lemoine, Algolia’s other co-founder, wrote a data-rich blog article comparing Algolia with its top competitor at the time. It was an earnest piece that spoke about instances where the competitor was better than Algolia and vice versa. The article which was well-researched with supporting data brought in consistent leads for a very long time. This generated tons of leads and credibility — before content marketing was even a consideration. The idea is to identify your superpower(s) and double down on it. Most SaaS startup founders have shiny object syndrome— they want to try events, blog articles, partner programs, outbound outreach all at once.

My list:
Slow it down if you don’t have a great co-founder

[Excerpt 4]
#10. Don’t Run Out of Money
.  The entire venture industry is under stress this year.  If you need a bridge round, discuss it — early.  Talk about it,  Talk about what to do if you have less than 18-24 months of runway.  Don’t just … run out of money.  You might laugh, but this is far too common.  Founders hide from running out of money, and/or plan way too optimistic financial plans that can’t realistically be hit.
To some, this will look like a very basic checklist.  But it isn’t, or at least, isn’t anymore.  Almost everyone stopped doing at least some or even all of this stuff.  But if you don’t, your investors are less likely to be there when you need them.  Not the best look these days.
answer_a:
We’ve talked a lot over the years on SaaStr about how to avoid running out of cash.  But perhaps we haven’t discussed the #1 thing I see CEOs and founders do to minimize their risk here.
Yes, burn management is important.  Yes, managing your runway is critical today.  Yes, making sure you know exactly when you’re going to run out of money matters.
But really, the #1 thing you can do to make sure you never run out of money?  Is just make sure you have enough money.  Enough capital.
This sounds simple, and it is.  But most folks forget to focus on this until it’s almost too late.  And the reality today is it’s hard to raise VC financing again.  And it’s harder to get a second check from VCs after you’ve raised your initial round.
So my advice is this: make sure you understand you have enough capital for the next 12+ months.  Even better, maybe find a way to stretch that to 24 months.  At least 15 months, minimum, though.
Now, let me add a couple practical tips:

#1. Don’t go into “low” deal mode if you aren’t 1000% sure you can close another round of funding.  If you are 80%-90% sure you can raise more money, stay in “high” deal mode.  Too many startups I invest in / advise went into low deal mode because they didn’t believe they could raise another round.  They did, but only after exhausting all options.  Stay positive here.
And finally — build up your war chest.  Raising too little capital is a huge trap.  Everyone runs out of money faster today.
answer_b:
We’re seeing a record number of startups seeking funding due to the “great AI boom”, which has led to an increase in competition for limited funds. However, here are my top tips to help you stand out during this competitive fundraising period.
Firstly, ensure you understand how much capital you really need
. Many founders make the mistake of raising more money than necessary, which can actually hurt their chances of securing investment. Instead, focus on getting a clear understanding of your startup’s cash requirements and only seek the amount needed to achieve your goals. #1. Hiring mediocre VPs instead of great ones
. This is perhaps the biggest mistake I see most founders make these days. There are simply too many startups these days. So no one is willing to take risks anymore. Everyone wants a VP with tons of experience, ideally at another start-up. But then they hire folks that … weren’t truly great at their last role. And maybe never were. These mediocre VPs don’t know how to recruit anyone good. They often break things in their area. And sometimes even worse, they create chaos when things go wrong. #2. Not raising enough capital
. Almost every VC fund is full. And yet there are always way too many startup founders underestimating how much money they really need. Most importantly, don’t raise less than you think you need. Because once you run out of cash … you lose. #3. Misunderstanding your competition
. There are probably 1000 reasons why you should win against your competitor(s). But I bet half those reasons won’t matter. Find out which 500 reasons count, and build around them. #4. Taking things personally
. When times got tough for us after YC Demo Day, I took it very personally. Why did people hate us? Wasn’t our app awesome? Etc. It wasn’t until I stepped back and looked at it objectively, that I realized we had a much bigger problem. Our product was pretty darn good. People hated us because our competitors were taking shots at us. In fact, they didn’t even tell the truth.

:
